sec.title: Background:
sec.p: Medicine stockouts (MSOs) remain a significant challenge to delivering quality health services in primary care, primarily due to inefficiencies in Medicine Supply Chain Management (MSCM). This study reviewed existing MSCM models and key factors to develop strategies for strengthening their implementation in primary care settings.

sec.title: Methods:
sec.p: A scoping review was conducted, including original studies published in the PubMed, Scopus, and EBSCO databases between January 2010 and January 2025. The included studies assessed pharmaceutical supply chain models or interventions addressing MSO in primary health care. Studies focused on industry supply chains, wholesalers, vaccines, or reviews were excluded. The Antecedent, Decision, and Outcome (ADO) method was used to lead a systematic scoping review. Antecedents were defined as factors associated with MSCM, decisions referred to the MSCM models, and outcomes represented their performance. Data were thematically analysed using the Pharmaceutical Management Framework, and the reported study followed PRISMA-ScR guidelines.

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: Out of 307 identified articles, 28 met the inclusion criteria. Some countries adopted digital solutions, such as stock tracking tools and Geographic Information Systems. At the same time, those with limited infrastructure focused on strengthening governance and supervision, such as through the Supervision, Performance Assessment, and Recognition Strategy. Contributing factors to MSOs include weaknesses in medicine management, inadequate managerial support, policy gaps, and external disruptions to the supply chain.

sec.title: Conclusion:
sec.p: Successful models for MSOs integrate key factors such as digital technology, strengthened human resource capacity, and supportive governance structures. Future strategies should prioritise systems that are adaptable, data-driven, and backed by strong government commitment.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Essential medications must be readily available for efficient healthcare delivery, particularly in primary health care (PHC) settings (Abdulah et al., 2014; Alemu et al., 2023; Sankaran, 2025). With recorded stockouts in Tanzania, 31% (Wiedenmayer et al., 2019), Indonesia, 42% (Fanda et al., 2024), Saudi Arabia, 48.5% (Alshibli et al., 2024), and the United States, 39% and Canada, 34% (Tadrous et al., 2024), medicine stockouts (MSOs) continue to be a global problem. Critical MSOs can disrupt treatment regimen, elevate morbidity, and even cause death (Alemu et al., 2023; Allaw et al., 2025). Additionally, they caused patients to become less compliant (46.4%), lose faith in medical professionals and medications (41.4%), and experience stress and frustration (44.3%) (Alshibli et al., 2024).

Several factors contribute to MSOs, including weak forecasting, poor inventory, suboptimal planning, prolonged procurement, and inadequate safety stock (Alemu et al., 2023; Davlantes et al., 2019; Kumar & Kumar, 2018; Leung et al., 2016; Zuma, 2022). A lack of technological integration in supply chain operations, logistical challenges, and political and economic instability have also been connected to persistent MSOs (Carolien et al., 2017). Strengthening Supply Chain Management (SCM) is therefore essential. Data-driven demand planning, distribution process optimisation, and risk management to foresee any supply chain interruptions are all components of effective supply chain management (Ivanov et al., 2019; Morris, 2018). A robust SCM system reduces MSOs, minimises expiration-related waste, and improves budget efficiency (Iqbal et al., 2017; Lugada et al., 2022).

However, challenges still exist in creating a paradigm for a sustainable pharmaceutical supply chain that successfully lowers MSO (Abdulkadir et al., 2024; Suparan et al., 2014). Several reviews related to MSOs have been conducted (Bahadori et al., 2024; Yenet et al., 2023); however, they focused on hospital or industrial supply chains (Iqbal et al., 2017; Mathur et al., 2018). While they quantify MSOs, they rarely analyse models or evaluate their effectiveness in reducing MSOs (Sagitasari et al., 2024; Santhireswaran et al., 2024; Wadhwa et al., 2024). Furthermore, most lack comprehensive frameworks incorporating determinants such as the medicine management cycle, management support, and regulatory context. Accordingly, this study aims to assess existing MSCM models and related aspects to identify prospective strategies for adopting qualified MSCM in primary health care (PHC) institutions. A qualified MSCM refers to a pharmaceutical supply chain model or system that demonstrates high performance outcomes, such as reducing medicine stockouts, improving medicine availability, and streamlining distribution. By highlighting best practices and identifying weaknesses in current approaches, this review seeks to provide strategic recommendations for strengthening MSCM implementation.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p:
PRISMA-ScR criteria were used to report on the findings (Levac et al., 2010). The included articles are specifically original studies on SCM to prevent MSOs in PHC. Eligible studies are those that identify the factors causing MSOs, evaluate SCM models, or analyze interventions and strategies aimed at improve medicine availability in primary health care. Each study had to map at least one of the Antecedents, Decisions, Outcomes (ADO) framework (Paul et al., 2024). Antecedents refer to initial factors or causes that occur before an event or outcome – causes of MSO. Decisions involve the policies, strategies, or managerial interventions chosen to address the problem; the SCM models used are examined. Outcomes refer to the results or impacts of the decisions made – SCM performance. The ADO framework was selected because it can systematically map the main factors leading to MSOs (antecedents), managerial interventions/decisions (SCM model), and the resulting outcomes (supply performance). In this context, antecedents refer to various factors that interact with each other and collectively contribute to MSOs, rather than a single event. The pharmaceutical management framework serves as the foundation for strengthening antecedents. sec.title: Search strategy
sec.p: Given the study’s focus on pharmacy management, drug supply chains, and health policy, the PubMed, Scopus, and EBSCO databases were used to obtain the relevant peer-reviewed literature within the scope of the scoping review. The complete search strategy is detailed in Supplemental Material Table S1. We included original English-language research that examined SCM and MSOs in PHC, covering influencing determinants, SCM models, SCM model performance, and strategies for addressing MSO published from January 2010 to January 2025. We excluded studies that focused on topics outside SCM (such as therapy management or pharmacovigilance), settings outside PHC (such as the pharmaceutical industry or wholesalers), and vaccine-related studies, book chapters, and reviews.

sec.title: Data collection and extraction
sec.p: All records were managed in Mendeley®, de-duplicated, and initially screened (titles, abstracts, and full texts) by the first author (FA). The screening and data extraction were performed using a standardised and piloted extraction matrix to systematically capture study characteristics, including authors/year, objectives, design, service level, geographic context (i.e. urban, rural, or both), commodity type (i.e. medicine, basic diagnostic tools, or both), and ADO-aligned elements. Although statistical inter-rater reliability was not calculated due to the single-reviewer approach, methodological rigour and reliability were enhanced through random verification by co-authors, independent consistency checks, and maintained audit trails to minimise potential bias.

sec.title: Data analysis
sec.p: All included studies were reviewed to identify determinants of MSO and strategies to prevent them. Through iterative team discussions, we synthesised findings, concise summaries, and grouped models, determinants, and outcomes by similarity. For interpretive structure, evidence was mapped onto the Pharmaceutical Management Framework (Quick, 2012) – medicine management cycle, management support, and policy/regulation. The reason for selecting the Pharmaceutical Management Framework is that it clearly depicts the pharmaceutical management cycle and aligns with the factors that influence MSO, enabling a structured relationship between ADO components and SCM performance.

sec.title: Study selection
sec.p:
The search yielded 307 articles; 70.62% (n = 149) were eliminated based on title and abstract. Of 62 full-text review, 34 were excluded for the following reasons (eleven book chapters, eight vaccine-focused, six on availability/delivery metrics without SCM determinants/models, three on perceptions/social impact only, two on unrelated topics (e.g. pharmacovigilance, AI data mining not SCM-related), two on industrial supply and distributors issue – not PHC SCM, and two review/report papers) – a total of 28 articles for further analysis (Figure 2). sec.title: Study characteristics
sec.p:
The 28 studies used diverse designs: cross-sectional, qualitative, mixed-method, implementation research, prospective longitudinal, machine learning-based stochastic models, and system dynamics modelling with data simulation. Settings spanned low-income nations (i.e. Ethiopia, Malawi, Mozambique, and South Sudan), lower-middle-income nations (i.e. Uganda, Ghana, Pakistan, Tanzania, India, Nigeria, and Rwanda), and upper-middle-income nations (i.e. Namibia, Indonesia, South Africa, and Brazil). Sixteen articles covered both urban and rural settings, with six articles focusing on each. Most studies were conducted at primary health care units/PHCUs (public health centres and primary hospitals) (n = 6) and public health centres (n = 13). Meanwhile, in other sectors such as private not-for-profit health settings, drug store departments, and public health centres; public and private health sectors; central medical stores (CMS) and the Ministry of Health; PHCUs and CMS; PHCUs, private pharmacies, district central warehouses; and primary health care clinics, there were 1–2 locations. Medicines (n = 19), medications with diagnostic tests (n = 6), and diagnostic tests (n = 3) were the commodities examined (Abdulkadir et al., 2024; Alemu et al., 2023; Berhanemeskel et al., 2016; Bhat et al., 2024; Chandani et al., 2012; Davlantes et al., 2019; Desale et al., 2013; Hailu & Mohammed, 2020; Hodes et al., 2017; Hussain et al., 2021; Hwang et al., 2019; Joosse et al., 2024; Kaupa & Naude, 2021; Kumar & Kumar, 2018; Kuupiel et al., 2019; Magadzire et al., 2014; Manyuat et al., 2021; Mikkelsen-Lopez et al., 2014; Mufadhol et al., 2023; Muyingo et al., 2022; Mwencha et al., 2017; Nakambale & Bangalee, 2022; Nascimento et al., 2017; Ruhago et al., 2022; Tessema et al., 2012; Trap et al., 2018; Umer et al., 2023; Wiedenmayer et al., 2019). sec.title: Determinant of medicine stockout (Antecedents)
sec.p:
Four themes and 14 subthemes appeared: (1) medicine management cycle, which was notable, with issues ranging from medicine selection, planning, distribution, and use; (2) management support, which was recognised as one of the key themes, encompassing four distinct subthemes: management information systems, funding system, human resources, and organisation; (3) policy, law, and regulation; (4) external systems and environmental factors, such as supplier issues, climate, global supply chain disruptions, imports, and donations. sec.title: Supply chain management models (Decisions)
sec.p:
Across several nations, MSCM models share common goals: increase access, decrease MSO, streamline distribution, and optimise logistical data use. Technology-driven models are utilised in countries with advanced technological capabilities, including machine learning stochastic models (MLSM) and Rule-Based reasoning methods (RbRM), dynamic system modelling (DSM), Field Report on Stock Tracker (FROST), and Geographic Information System (GIS) under the Medical Access Uganda Limited Procurement and Supply Chain Strengthening Project (MAUL PSSP) (Bhat et al., 2024; Kumar & Kumar, 2018; Mufadhol et al., 2023; Muyingo et al., 2022). Models like the Integrated Pharmaceutical Logistics System (IPLS) and Logistics Management Information System (LMIS) explicitly highlight the importance of the information systems of logistics reporting and tracking in enabling effective medicine stock management (Alemu et al., 2023; Mwencha et al., 2017). In contrast, countries with limited technological infrastructure emphasise strengthening governance and supervision models, as seen in the Supervision, Performance Assessment and Recognition Strategy (SPARS), Mentorship and Technical Health Systems Strengthening (MaTHSS) under MAUL PSSP, Drug Revolving Fund (DRF), the Jazia Prime Vendor System (PVS), and Supply Chain for Community Case Management (SC4CCM) (Abdulkadir et al., 2024; Davlantes et al., 2019; Muyingo et al., 2022; Trap et al., 2018; Wiedenmayer et al., 2019). sec.title: Performance of supply chain management models (Outcomes)
sec.p: Ten MSCM models showed a positive SCM impact. DRF, MLSM, RbRM, LMIS, SC4CCM, Jazia PVS, DSM, MAUL PSSP, and SPARS improved medicine availability and reduced MSO. LMIS reduced MSO from 45% to 22% (Mwencha et al., 2017), MAUL PSSP from 46% to 4% with stock adequacy rising from 54% to 71% (Muyingo et al., 2022). The Jazia PVS increased tracer medicine availability 69% to 94% (Wiedenmayer et al., 2019). The SPARS improved management capacity by 70% in one year (Trap et al., 2018). IPLS improved the efficiency of tracking and logistics information but did not report explicit availability outcomes (Alemu et al., 2023). Ultimately, the results show that most of the SCM models examined improve medication availability by enhancing data use, strengthening logistics management systems, and implementing strategies to address distribution issues across different healthcare settings. Detailed SCM model performances are presented in Table 2.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The key findings of this review were that the medicine management cycle, management support, regulations/policies, and external factors were the antecedents of MSO. To address this, various models have been implemented in multiple countries (decisions), including those based on technology-driven approaches (MLSM, DSM, FRoST, and GIS, which is part of MAUL PSSP), information systems (LMIS and IPLS), and governance and supervision (SPARS, MaTHSS, also part of MAUL PSSP, Jazia PVS, DRF, and SC4CCM). All models showed strong effectiveness in preventing MSO (outcomes).

A critical weakness in the medicine management cycle lies in procurement and distribution. Procurement challenges include demand forecasting, bureaucratic processes, and lengthy processes (Abdulkadir et al., 2024; Alemu et al., 2023; Berhanemeskel et al., 2016; Hailu & Mohammed, 2020; Kaupa & Naude, 2021; Kumar & Kumar, 2018; Mufadhol et al., 2023). Strengthening inventory management is therefore essential to prevent MSO (Uthayakumar & Priyan, 2013). A key strategy is improving requirement planning by analyzing usage trends and historical demand data (Bialas et al., 2020).

Several models illustrate practical approaches. Information system-based models like LMIS and technology-driven models like MLSM support data-driven procurement by strengthening logistics data collection, analysis, and use in decision-making. LMIS has been implemented in urban and rural areas in Tanzania and Ethiopia, and has reduced MSO from 45% to 22% (Desale et al., 2013; Mwencha et al., 2017). MLSM, which has been deployed in rural and urban community health clinics in India, has proven to be extremely effective at correctly estimating demand (Bhat et al., 2024). By managing inventory and forecasting demand using data analysis and predictive models, the risk of MSO and overstocking can be decreased (Ogbewele et al., 2024).

Geographical and transportation obstacles, MSO in national and regional warehouses, a lack of traceability, opaque data, and inadequate infrastructure are some of the distribution challenges. Several models help address these issues. Last-mile distribution is improved through governance and supervision models, such as SC4CCM, which train community health workers (CHWs) to deliver medications to remote and hard-to-reach areas (Chandani et al., 2012; Davlantes et al., 2019). Technology-driven models, such as RbRM, enable facilities to request medicine directly, improving distribution efficiency and reducing dependence on the central warehouse (Mufadhol et al., 2023).

The main management support problems involve human resources (HR) and the management information system (MIS). Core HR issues include shortages of health workers and inadequate drug management skills (Hailu & Mohammed, 2020; Kaupa & Naude, 2021). Governance and supervision models such as SPARS and MaTHSS have demonstrated effectiveness. SPARS deploys trained medicines management supervisors to oversee facilities and monitor stock, storage, ordering, prescribing, and dispensing. In Uganda, it achieved >70% median improvement within the first year across government and non-profit facilities (Trap et al., 2018). The MaTHSS model combines on-site mentorship, LMIS and SCM training, and supervision, resulting in a 12% increase in drug inventory accuracy from 79% to 91% (Muyingo et al., 2022).

MIS problems include reliance on manual stock systems, weak procurement, and a lack of digital monitoring across the supply chain. Digital inventory systems can enhance stock visibility, support procurement, and distribution decision-making (Wong et al., 2023). Inventory management is improved by models such as DSM and MAUL PSSP. In Uganda, MAUL PSSP successfully reduced MSO from 46% to 4% using FROST and GIS tools to visualise stock status (Muyingo et al., 2022). In India, DSM improved medicine stock management by modelling inventory behaviour over time and serving as a forecasting tool for decision-makers, demonstrating significant improvement in rural medicine availability (Kumar & Kumar, 2018).

Regulatory limitations, weak policy enforcement, and poor supply chain governance contribute to MSO (Abdulkadir et al., 2024; Kaupa & Naude, 2021; Wiedenmayer et al., 2019). Preventive strategies include stronger inventory control, stakeholder collaboration, and resilience governance (Lee, 2011). In Nigeria, compliance systems, diversifying suppliers, and regulatory engagement reduced MSO (Uchechukwu, 2024). In Europe, regulatory scarcity challenges required EU-level cooperation, with harmonised communication, risk assessment, and management to mitigate MSO (Musazzi et al., 2020).

External factors, including imports, donations, suppliers, climate change, and disasters, also drive MSO. Reliance on imports, weak local production, and global outsourcing heighten vulnerabilities, while extreme weather and COVID-19 lockdowns worsened disruptions (Busola, 2024; Hussain et al., 2021; Nakambale & Bangalee, 2022; Umer et al., 2023). Mitigation strategies include expanding suppliers, developing regional manufacturing hubs (Sanket & Ankitkumar, 2024), and leveraging technologies to enhance visibility and resilience (Elbeltagy et al., 2022). Integrating these measures supports a flexible framework to reduce MSO in PHC. Figure 3 illustrates determinants, sub-determinants, and strategies for preventing drug stockouts.

A comparative analysis of the identified MSCM models revealed that the technology-based approach is the most effective at enhancing forecasting accuracy, inventory stability, and data visibility. Still, it requires significant digital infrastructure and technical skills, limiting its transferability to primary care facilities with fewer resources. Information system-based models offer a balance between effectiveness and efficiency, reducing stockout and operational costs by improving data integration and reporting, while maintaining moderate adaptability across contexts. On the other hand, governance and oversight models demonstrate the greatest transferability and sustainability, effectively improving managerial capacity, accountability, and procurement transparency while requiring less reliance on technology. Integrating all of the models sequentially – governance and oversight as a foundation, information systems to reinforce data, and digital innovation gradually – emerges as the most practical strategy for improving supply chain resilience and ensuring sustainable drug availability in primary health care.

According to the WHO global framework on equitable access to essential medicines, equitable access relies on four interrelated pillars: rational use of medicines, affordable prices, sustainable financing, and reliable health and supply systems (Organization, W. H., 2004). In this context, none of the identified MSCM models fully cover all four pillars; however, MAUL PSSP and Jazia PVS showed the highest level of integration. The MAUL PSSP model – through components such as MaTHSS, FRoST, GIS, and WhatsApp Ordering – improves rational use, affordability, sustainable financing, and supply reliability by combining governance reform, digital innovation, and workforce strengthening (Muyingo et al., 2022). Similarly, the Jazia PVS public–private partnership promotes rational procurement, transparent pricing, cost-sharing mechanisms, and dependable distribution (Wiedenmayer et al., 2019). Together, these models exemplify multidimensional, scalable strategies aligned with the WHO’s framework for strengthening the resilience of the pharmaceutical supply chain in primary health care.

The findings of this review offer practical insights and frameworks that policymakers can adopt to strengthen supply chain governance, improve medicine availability, and enhance system resilience. To advance this agenda, standardised, comparable outcome indicators across sites should be used rigorously to evaluate supply chain interventions in future studies. Longitudinal and implementation studies that assess the efficacy and economic viability of MSCM models are also needed.

sec.title: Strengths and limitations
sec.p: This review's ability to systematically map the models, performance, factors, and strategies influencing MSOs in PHC is one of its key strengths. The Pharmacy Management Framework was used for analysis, while the ADO framework supported the review. However, differences in how studies define stockouts and performance indicators may affect comparability, limiting causal conclusions about the effectiveness. Therefore, the result should be interpreted carefully.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: The MSCM models discussed in this review range from technology-based approaches and information system-based approaches to governance and oversight models, with varying levels of complexity. The effectiveness of each MSCM model depends on several key factors, such as the drug management cycle, management support, and policies and regulations. Successful models typically accelerate the adoption of digital tools, standardise recording and reporting, enhance human resource capabilities, and promote stakeholder coordination.
